steps.explanationAfterStep: E2: the β-hydrogen sits on the outside of the molecule where the bulky base can reach it. Bulky bases are used on purpose when an alkene, not a substitution product, is wanted.

title: 1-Bromopropane and tert-butoxide
subtitle: Primary, bulky base: elimination
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapters 15 and 17

reactants.caption: potassium tert-butoxide + 1-bromopropane
hintTiers: The substrate is primary, but look at the base. Can something this bulky reach the back of a carbon?
A bulky base takes a proton instead: E2. The oxygen takes the drawn hydrogen, the C–H electrons form the π bond, and bromide leaves. Three arrows.
tert-Butoxide oxygen lone pair → the drawn hydrogen; that C–H bond → a π bond to the carbon carrying bromine; the C–Br bond → a lone pair on bromine.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Substitution or elimination? Draw the main pathway.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: With ethoxide this SN2 would be the main pathway. tert-Butoxide is too bulky to reach the back of the carbon, so it removes a proton instead: E2.
The base attacks a hydrogen, not the electron-rich bromine.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the base takes the proton. Now the C–H electrons form the C=C π bond, pushing bromide out.

mechanismSummary: The carbon carrying bromine is primary, so SN2 would be easy for a small nucleophile. tert-Butoxide is too bulky to reach the back of the C–Br bond, but it can still take an exposed β-hydrogen: E2 gives propene as the main product.
